paper.title_en: Quantum and Classical Memory for Storage and Retrieval of Quantum Measurements
paper.abstract_en: We study the persistent quantum and classical memory required for exact heralded storage and retrieval of quantum measurements. Given only black-box access to the measurement channel, we construct an exact compression of the port-based program into an outcome-type record and a quantum register, with total dimension polynomial in the query count. For every universal retrieval processor we prove the bounds $Q+C\ge\log_2 n$ and $2Q+C\ge\log_2\bigl((n-1)d^2+1\bigr)$ on the numbers $Q$ of qubits and $C$ of bits of the program, for $n$-outcome POVMs on $\mathbb{C}^d$ with $d\ge2$. For $n\ge2$, no finite classical memory removes the need for quantum memory: any such processor requires a quantum program of dimension at least $d$, at that dimension its classical alphabet must have at least $n$ symbols, and both minima are attained by a single-query protocol with success $1/d^2$. Combining direct-program compression with a converse from approximate measurement programming gives logarithmic total-memory scaling in $1/(1-p)$ as the uniform success probability $p$ approaches one, at fixed $d,n\ge2$. At fixed input dimension and target success below one, the optimal total-memory scaling is logarithmic in $n$. We also construct self-contained programs under branch-decomposition access and compare the quantum and classical costs of all constructions, including where the outcome-type record is kept: for POVMs with $n$ nonzero rank-one effects the direct program admits a purely quantum allocation whose register is never larger than that of the minimal-Naimark unitary program and which succeeds more often whenever $n>d$.
